instruction.what: Step 3.1, the elements of one subgroup (stage 4, C1; the end of the loop for the subgroup): what the evidence of the subgroup shows of the elements of a behaviour of the inner being. The input is the evidence observations of the subgroup by marker (`to_take_up`, the senses first, then the 2.1 findings and the older evidence), not the verses; the verses are kept for an occasional read-back. A finding is a building block, never a claim about the behaviour as a whole (that is stage 5).
read: Read the observations to take up, in order: the senses (1.1) and their enrichments (1.2) first, then the 2.1 findings (pairings, qualifiers, entities, direction, double meanings), then the older evidence. The inner-being workings work more with the senses than with the surfaces, so findings rest on the senses first.

For each item a finding may use (`uses`): what is done and its mode (operation, with its chain), whether a refusal or a pursuit (polarity), what it is directed at (object), the outward act (enactment), the other party with the route (party), the circumstance, and what a qualifier or a variation of the word gives the working (role, the dimension). Never the meaning of the word (stage 1).

Read the older inner-being observations (`older_inner_being`) with them: each is considered first, accepted with a trace to evidence, restated where it says more than the evidence, consumed where a finding says the same, merged, or deleted where it cannot be made true.
Go back to a verse (`verses`) only where the evidence does not settle the question, and say why.
write: Fill `answer.findings`: each one observation, with a `key` unique in the answer, `kind` (of the item's kinds), `text`, `basis` (stated or read), `parts` with `item` (one of `uses`) and what the item needs (with `grounds`), and `nodes`: a `traced` node on each observation it rests on (from `to_take_up` or `may_rest_on_besides`) and an `occurrence` node, with its `role` chosen from the verse (characteristic, qualifier, object, relational target, enactment or standalone), on the occurrences those observations cover.
An occurrence outside the observations a finding rests on is allowed only with a `read_back` entry on the finding: {verse: the osis id, why}.
`not_used`: {observation id: reason} for every observation to take up that no finding rests on. Every one is rested on or declared, never both.

`older`: answer, once, each older inner-being observation (`older_inner_being`) that has a node on an occurrence your findings name (RW-13; the record lists any it misses, and refuses an answer to one on no named occurrence: those are shown, not demanded, IB-05): keep (with nature inner_being: it stands, traced to evidence), restate, merge, consume (carriers ["this"] or ids, mapping), delete_neither, or defer (collection, nature, finding).
`existing`: answer every earlier reading (`earlier_readings`: inner being of an earlier grouping on these occurrences) with accept, modify, delete, merge or leave, and its reason.
The text says what the evidence shows of the element; it names its verses; it never restates a verse and never states the behaviour as a whole.
Then: Collection-Build.ps1 -Action RecordElements -File <the answer file> (-Check to preview). The record refuses the whole file on any fault and lists every fault.

keep.text: Stage 4 starts from the observations, not the verses (researcher, #2526 Q7, 2026-11-21): the subgroups and the stage 3 observations on them are the input, the behaviours are discovered from analysing them, and the base data is read back into only occasionally. Every finding of step 3.1 or 3.2 rests on named observations (a traced node on each, with an occurrence node as well) and its occurrence nodes lie within the occurrences those observations cover; an occurrence outside them is allowed only where the finding records a read-back (the verse and why). Each node has a role from reading.node_roles other than lexical, chosen by the reading. A 3.3 finding carries nodes on the occurrences of both sides in the shared verses.

A finding of a stage 4 row is checked by the rules of observationrecord.check and check_item_parts (kind, text, basis, route, parts.item and what the item needs, node roles, collection of each node) and by RG, RW and RS, which are not restated here: one observation for each finding, never a duplicate, with a node on each word it applies to (RO11, RW-03); founded in the observations and never a restatement of the verse (B:131); parts.item is one of the items the row's item uses (cfg_setting layer.reading). An observation whose nodes all bear on an act is refused: those words are nodes of the observation of the act. A finding is a building block of a behaviour and never a claim (stage 5).

Nothing the step reads is lost on the way to stage 5. Step 3.1: every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared in not_used with its reason in words. Step 3.2: every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour (a traced node on it from a flag finding of type discovery) or declared in not_gathered with its reason, and the row has at least one behaviour unless it is recorded as none with its reason. A behaviour names and gathers; it makes no claim about what the behaviour is.

An earlier inner-being observation with a node on the occurrences of a 3.1 row (any stage but those of the build: lexical, layer-1, layer-2, layer-3.1 to layer-3.3, and layer-3 before 2026-11-26) is shown in the pull for information and may be actioned in `existing`: accepted, modified, deleted, merged or left, each with its reason, through observationrecord (RW-01, RW-09); nothing is demanded of it, and it counts for nothing in the check. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason. Every older live observation with a node on an occurrence of the row is answered in fill.older at the record of the row (RW-13); this rule's `existing` actions of stage 4 are unchanged.

Every live observation marked inner_being holds at least one live traced node on a live observation marked evidence, or on a live inner-being observation that itself traces to evidence (the trace chain of stage 4: a 3.2 behaviour traces the 3.1 elements it gathers, a 3.3 match the 3.1 and 3.2 observations it comes from; at most three links), unless it is recorded self-evidencing: it quotes its verse in full and holds a word node for every word it relies on. A traced node never points at a deleted observation. A trace points first at existing evidence; an evidence observation is created only when none states the fact and it states what the nodes and the quotation do not. An inner-being observation traced to evidence not yet marked is pending, not failed.

Find the main inner-being operation, and give every word that bears on it its role in this finding (cfg_setting reading.node_roles): characteristic, qualifier and what it gives the characteristic, object or content, relational target, or enactment. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being is standalone. The role comes from this verse, never from the cluster tag. Where a standalone word proves to qualify a characteristic, it is a qualifier of it.

A qualifier gets no separate account of itself, but what it gives the characteristic it binds to is evaluated for its value and recorded as a qualification finding, applied by its nodes to the qualifier (role qualifier) and the characteristic (role characteristic). What it gives can vary widely: grade, nature, impact, size, relation, a measure, strengthening, ground, cause, object, setting or bait are examples, not a list (#2273 D9). A qualifier whose usage varies across contexts may earn its own reading later.

Record the parties: who bears the act, who causes it, who is acted on (source, target, impact, purpose), and the route (cfg_enum observation_route), whose meaning is cfg_behaviour_rule 72 (route-verses-hib-other-beings-data-only): A another being in its own right, B another being with the human inner being, C no bearing, data only; a verse may take A and B. A non-human being is never itself a HIB; a collective stays one HIB; an implied party is named as referential, never asserted.
Never close a verse or item on 'not X'. A role label is never a verdict; the close records what the verse is. Silence about the inner being is a finding, recorded as data with its reason.
A phenomenon hidden behind a stated or refrained act may be named, with the verb, clause or stated silence that grounds it, and whether it is stated or read.
Keep the source of an interior state apart from the source of an enablement to act.

A tagged word that works adverbially in an occurrence (a noun with a preposition qualifying the predicate, as 'in the counsel of the wicked') is a qualifier there, not the verse's characteristic. The role is per occurrence: the same word may be the characteristic elsewhere.
In a simile, the predicates of the vehicle (the tree that yields, does not wither) are read for what they say of the one compared (the tenor), not as the vehicle's own acts.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.

An observation is created with its marker (ib_observation.nature, from the item answered, cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature; a finding file never sets it) and every word node with the columns of layer.reading node_required. A column the data cannot give (layer.reading node_gap_columns: an empty morph in the source row, a surface with no placement in the collection index) is left empty and its reason is kept on the node (disposition_note); any other missing column refuses the whole file and nothing is written. A trace to a deleted observation is refused (IB-07).

Evidence states what the data are or show, tied to a verse. Inner being states how something works in the inner being, based on evidence, a building block of the stage 5 claims. The marker (ib_observation.nature) follows the content and purpose of the observation, never its stage (RS-04): an observation of any stage may be inner being when it traces to evidence. One that states both is split. The marker is set when the observation is created, by the item that is answered (cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature); a finding file never sets it; the validation changes it only where the content shows the item's nature does not hold.

The study's primary focus is the human inner being (HIB). Each verse read is routed by what it shows, and the route is recorded in its observation. (A) Other beings in their own right: a word used of God, angels, other spirits or nature (non-HIB) is routed to Ch 13 "Other beings" (13.1 Divine, 13.2 Angels, 13.3 Other spirits, 13.4 Nature), read for what the verses say that being is and does; for God, also how his character passed to the HIB through creation in his image, held open (#1984). (B) Another being interacting with the HIB is fully in HIB scope. A verse may take A and B, described from different angles. (C) A verse with no inner-being and no other-being bearing is still assessed and recorded as data, and does not enter the narrative.

to_take_up.text: Boasting: speaking with pride of a ground one claims, as verb and as noun. It holds whatever the ground is: one's own work or standing (2Cor 10:8, Rom 2:17), wealth and might (Psa 49:6, Jer 9:23), evil (Psa 52:1), idols (Psa 97:7), the flesh (Gal 6:13), tomorrow (Pro 27:1, Jam 4:16), another church (2Cor 9:2), weakness (2Cor 12:9); and the boast that is excluded (Rom 3:27, 1Cor 1:29) or denied of

The ground of the boast: the noun names the thing gloried in rather than the act, a person, a work or a state that is one's boast: the Corinthians and Paul to one another (2Cor 1:14, 1Th 2:19), the testimony of conscience (2Cor 1:12), a ground Paul will not lose (1Cor 9:15), the reason in one's own tested work (Gal 6:4), the hope held fast (Heb 3:6), Egypt as Judah's glory (Isa 20:5).

Magnifying oneself over another: verbs of making great or glorifying oneself, with 'over' or 'against', rendered 'boast': Moab and Ammon over God's people and land (Zep 2:8, Zep 2:10), enemies over a man who slips (Psa 38:16), Edom over Judah (Obd 12), Israel over the Lord and the axe over the hewer (Judg 7:2, Isa 10:15), superiority with jealousy (Jam 3:14), the boastful and the lifted horn (Psa

Boastful talk: words of the mouth named as boasts, where the codes say speech, mouth or empty talk and the context makes them inflated or hollow: the mouth speaking swollen things (Jude 16), Moab's false boasts (Jer 48:30), the sayings people approve (Psa 49:13), the evildoers' speech beside arrogant words (Psa 94:4).

Glorying in God or in what he gives: the boast made in the Lord, his cross or his gift: in God continually beside thanks (Psa 44:8), the soul's boast in the Lord with the humble glad (Psa 34:2), knowing the Lord (Jer 9:24), boast in the Lord (1Cor 1:31, 2Cor 10:17), only in the cross (Gal 6:14), the lowly in his exaltation (Jam 1:9), entering into the nations' glory (Isa 61:6).

Boasting is borne out by G2744 (to boast, brag about, glory in; proper or improper by its object) with its nouns G2745 and G2746, by G6094 and G4068 (to boast, brag, vaunt oneself; Jam 3:5, 1Cor 13:4) and by H1984H in the Hithpael (to boast, make one's boast; Psa 52:1, Jer 9:23). G2745 adds the thing boasted of where G2746 is the act (1Cor 5:6 beside Rom 3:27). Two codes do not bear the sense out:

The ground of the boast is borne out by G2745, the thing to boast about, a ground or matter of glorying (1Cor 9:15, Gal 6:4, 2Cor 1:14), with G2746 in the same use where the noun names what is boasted of (2Cor 1:12, 1Th 2:19), and by H8597, beauty, glory, which includes glorying and boasting (Isa 20:5). The Greek nouns name what is gloried in; the Hebrew names its splendour.

Magnifying oneself over another is borne out by H1431 in the Hiphil and Hithpael (to make great, to magnify oneself; Zep 2:8, Psa 38:16), by H6286A in the Hithpael (to glorify oneself, get glory to oneself; Judg 7:2, Isa 10:15) and by G2620 (to boast against, glory over, assume superiority over; Jam 3:14). H6310G is the mouth made great with H1431 at Obd 12. H1984C is to act madly, act like a madm

Boastful talk is borne out by H0907, empty talk, idle talk, lie (Jer 48:30), by H0559 in the Hithpael, to boast, to act proudly, on a verb of saying (Psa 94:4), and by G5246, swelling, pompous, boastful, with G2980, to speak (Jude 16). H6310I is the mouth as organ of speech (Psa 49:13): the lexicon names speech, and the boast is the ESV's rendering of it.

Glorying in God is borne out by G2744 in its other range, to rejoice in, glory in, rejoice, exult (1Cor 1:31, Gal 6:14, Jam 1:9), and by H1984H in the Piel, to praise, beside the Hithpael to glory, make one's boast (Psa 44:8, Psa 34:2, Jer 9:24). H3235 is to exchange, in the Hithpael to enter into (Isa 61:6): the lexicon does not give boasting, and the sense rests there on the ESV's rendering.

In 2Cor 11:16 and 2Cor 12:6 thinking is how others rate Paul, and boasting is what he weighs doing: let no one count him a fool, and he refrains from boasting so that no one thinks more of him than he sees.

The surface boast carries the codes of boasting proper: G2744 in the New Testament (Rom 2:17, 1Cor 1:31, 2Cor 10:13, Jam 4:16), G4068 (1Cor 13:4) and G2620, boasting against (Jam 3:14); and H1984H in the Hithpael in the Old (Psa 52:1, Jer 9:23, Pro 27:1). These are one face: the word as the act of boasting, its ground named by the preposition that follows (in, of, about, against).

In 2Cor 1:14, 2Cor 5:12 and Gal 6:4 the surface boast carries G2745, in 2Cor 1:12 G2746 and in Isa 20:5 H8597: a noun for the thing gloried in, not the act; Isa 20:5 names a nation as the boast, beside its hope.

In Psa 38:16, Obd 12, Judg 7:2 and Isa 10:15 the surface boast carries verbs of making great or glorifying oneself (H1431, H6286A) and, at Obd 12, the noun mouth (H6310G) with H1431: the face is a self-magnifying over another, marked by over or against.
In Psa 94:4 the surface boast carries H0559, a verb of saying (Hithpael): the face is speech about oneself, set beside the arrogant words poured out.
In Psa 75:4 the surface boast carries H1984C, the verb of acting madly or foolishly: the face is folly, set in parallel with lifting the horn.
In Isa 61:6 the surface boast carries H3235, to exchange or to enter into: the face is coming into the nations' glory, which the ESV renders as boasting.
In 2Cor 11:21 the surface boast stands where the code is G5111, to dare, twice: the face is daring, and the boast is supplied by the English from 11:16-18.

The surface boasted carries three codes in three verses: in Psa 44:8 H1984H in the Piel, praise made in God; in Zep 2:10 H1431, a making great over God's people; in 2Cor 11:12 G2744, the opponents' boast in their work. This finding is the face of Psa 44:8, the boast that is praise.
In Zep 2:10 the surface boasted carries H1431, a verb of making great with against: the face of boasted that is self-magnifying over another people, apart from its use in Psa 44:8 and 2Cor 11:12.
In 2Cor 11:12 the surface boasted carries G2744 as a finite verb the ESV turns into an adjective: the face of boasted that is a claim made for one's own work, apart from Psa 44:8 and Zep 2:10.

In Jude 16 the surface boasters spans two codes in one verse: G2980, the verb to speak with the mouth as subject, and G5246, the swollen things spoken. The English noun for persons stands on a Greek clause about inflated speech; the surface has no other verse.

The surface boasting carries the noun of the thing gloried in, G2745 in 1Cor 9:15, 1Cor 9:16 and Heb 3:6 and G2746 in 1Th 2:19: a ground for boasting, the boasting held with hope, the crown of boasting. This is its face as the matter boasted of.

The surface boasting carries the noun of the act, G2746 in Rom 3:27, 2Cor 7:14, 2Cor 8:24, 2Cor 11:10 and Jam 4:16, and G2745 in the same use in 1Cor 5:6 and 2Cor 9:3: boasting as something made, said and judged. This is its face as the act.

In 2Cor 10:16 and 2Cor 12:1 the surface boasting carries the verb G2744 as an infinitive (aorist and present): the face of boasting as Paul's own act, refused in another's area and continued under necessity.

The surface boasts carries H1984H in Psa 10:3, Pro 20:14, Pro 25:14 and Jer 9:24, the Hebrew verb of boasting in Piel and Hithpael: the face of boasts as the act, of craving, of a bargain, of a gift not given, and of knowing the Lord.

In Psa 10:3 the surface boasts is also stored on H3588A, the conjunction for or that, which opens the verse: a word of no boasting meaning carried by the surface, a data error in the tagging of the surface (data-error).
In Psa 49:13 and Jer 48:30 the surface boasts carries nouns of speech, H6310I mouth and H0907 empty talk: the face of boasts as words said, approved by those after them or declared false.
In Zep 2:8 the surface boasts carries H1431, the verb of making great with against: the face of boasts as self-magnifying over the land of another people.

In 1Cor 1:31, 2Cor 7:14 and 2Cor 10:17 the surface boasts carries G2744 and in Jam 3:5 G6094: the Greek verbs of boasting, the one who boasts in the Lord, a boast made to Titus, and the tongue boasting of great things.

A negator reaches the boast itself: the jussive or imperative with not forbids it (1Ki 20:11, Psa 75:4, Pro 27:1, Jer 9:23, Obd 12, Jam 3:14), no one or no flesh excludes the one who would boast (1Cor 1:29, 1Cor 3:21, Eph 2:9), it is denied of love (1Cor 13:4), the ground is denied (1Cor 9:16), and not ... except, or far be it ... except, leaves one object only (2Cor 12:5, Gal 6:14). Adjectives and words of quantity stand with the boast, on its subject or its ground: too many (Judg 7:2), the humble who hear (Psa 34:2), the abundance of riches (Psa 49:6), those after them (Psa 49:13), arrogant words (Psa 94:4), bad, bad, then (Pro 20:14), faithless (Jer 49:4), last year and most (2Cor 9:2), all (2Th 1:4), lowly (Jam 1:9), small against great things (Jam 3:5), all and evil (Jam

God, the Lord, or the Lord Jesus Christ is named as the one boasted in, after in or with the content of knowing him: Psa 34:2, Psa 44:8, Jer 9:24, Rom 2:17, 1Cor 1:31, 2Cor 10:17, and Gal 6:14 (the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ).

may_rest_on_besides.text: In 2Cor 11:12 the verb is present middle, third plural, and its subject is the opponents Paul means to undermine: what they boast of is their work, claimed to be on the same terms as his. The ESV turns the finite verb into the adjective 'boasted' on 'mission', so the English hides that the boasting is their own present act.

In Zep 2:10 the Hiphil of the verb of making great (wayyiqtol, third plural) is rendered 'boasted'. With 'against the people of the Lord' and beside 'taunted', it says Moab and Ammon made themselves great over God's people; the English narrows a verb of magnifying to speech.

In Psa 44:8 the Piel perfect (first plural) has God as the ground of the boast ('in God'), and it stands parallel to giving thanks to his name forever: the people's boast here is praise of God, made continually.

In Jude 16 the verb of speaking (present active, third singular) has the mouth as its subject; it is part of the Greek phrase the ESV renders 'loud-mouthed boasters'. The Greek says the mouth speaks swollen things; the English makes a noun for a kind of person out of a verb of speech.

In Jude 16 the adjective (accusative plural neuter) is the object of the verb of speaking: what the mouth utters is swollen, oversized. Joined to that verb it is rendered 'loud-mouthed boasters'; the literal sense is words inflated beyond their size, and the ESV moves it from the words to the speakers.

In 2Cor 10:16 the aorist infinitive is negated by 'without': Paul's purpose is to preach beyond the Corinthians and not to boast of work already done in another's area of influence. The object of the boast is another's labour, and it is what he refuses.
In 2Cor 12:1 the present infinitive depends on 'I must': Paul's boasting goes on under necessity, though he says nothing is gained by it, and it leads into visions and revelations of the Lord.
In 1Cor 9:15 and 9:16 the noun names the ground or matter of boasting: Paul would rather die than lose it (9:15), and preaching itself gives him none, because necessity is laid on him (9:16).

In 1Cor 5:6 and 2Cor 9:3 the noun names the boast as made and held: the Corinthians' boast, judged not good beside the leaven that leavens the lump (1Cor 5:6), and Paul's boast about the Corinthians, which he fears may prove empty (2Cor 9:3).
In Heb 3:6 the noun stands with 'confidence' as what the believers hold fast, and its object is 'our hope': the boast is something kept and possessed, the condition of being God's house.

In 2Cor 7:14 and 8:24 the noun is Paul's boasting about the Corinthians made before Titus and the brothers; it is tested by their conduct: before Titus it proved true (7:14), and the Corinthians are asked to give proof of it (8:24).
In 2Cor 11:10 the noun is Paul's own boasting, bound to the truth of Christ in him; he states that no one will stop it in Achaia.
In Rom 3:27 the noun is 'our boasting', asked after and declared excluded, not by a law of works but by the law of faith.
In Jam 4:16 the noun gathers the boasting just named, a boast made in arrogance about plans for tomorrow, and judges all of it evil.

In 1Th 2:19 the noun is in the genitive after 'crown': a crown of boasting before the Lord at his coming, and the answer to 'what is' it is the Thessalonians themselves. The boast is a person, held up before the Lord.

In 1Cor 1:31 and 2Cor 10:17 the present participle with the article names 'the one who boasts', and the same verb then commands where that boast is to be made: in the Lord. Both are a citation ('as it is written').
In 2Cor 7:14 the perfect (first singular) is a boast Paul has made to Titus about the Corinthians, and he states he was not put to shame by it.

In Jam 3:5 the verb (present active, third singular) has the tongue as its subject and 'great things' as its object; the verse sets the small member against what it boasts of, and against the fire that sets a forest ablaze.

In Jer 48:30 the noun (masculine plural, construct with 'his') is rendered 'boasts'; its sense is empty or idle talk. The Lord declares Moab's boasts false and pairs them with his deeds and his insolence, so the boast is talk with nothing behind it.

In Zep 2:8 the Hiphil of the verb of making great (wayyiqtol, third plural) with 'against their territory' is rendered 'made boasts': Moab and Ammon magnified themselves over the land of God's people. The verse sets it beside taunts and revilings the Lord has heard.
In Psa 10:3 the subject is the wicked and the object of the boast is his own craving, what his soul desires; and the verse sets it beside the greedy man who curses and renounces the Lord.

In Pro 20:14 and Pro 25:14 the boast stands against what was said or done: the buyer who called the goods bad boasts once he goes away (20:14), and a man who boasts of giving what he never gives is likened to clouds and wind without rain (25:14).
In Jer 9:24 the one who boasts is told what to boast in: that he understands and knows the Lord, who practises steadfast love, justice and righteousness; the boast is given its proper object.

In Psa 49:13 the noun is 'mouth' (construct, with 'their'), rendered 'boasts': people after them approve what the foolish say. The English names as boasts what the Hebrew calls their mouth, their sayings.

In Jam 3:14 the present imperative (second plural) of the verb of boasting against is forbidden where bitter jealousy and selfish ambition are in the heart, and it is joined to being false to the truth.

In 1Cor 1:31, 2Cor 10:17 and Gal 6:14 the boast is given its object outside the self: the imperative of the citation (1Cor 1:31, 2Cor 10:17) commands it to be made in the Lord, and Paul refuses any boast except in the cross of Christ (Gal 6:14).

In Rom 2:17 and Rom 2:23 the boast is in God and in the law, made by one who relies on the law; the verse of 2:23 says the one who boasts in the law dishonours God by breaking it, so the boast and the conduct go apart.

In 1Cor 1:29, Eph 2:9, 1Cor 3:21 and 1Cor 4:7 the boast is excluded or forbidden: no human being may boast before God (1Cor 1:29), salvation does not come from works, which leaves no room for a boast (Eph 2:9), no one is to boast in men (1Cor 3:21), and no one should boast of what he received as though he had not (1Cor 4:7).

In 2Cor 5:12, 2Cor 11:18 (the first verb) and Gal 6:13 the boast rests on the flesh or the outward appearance: those who boast of appearance and not of the heart (2Cor 5:12), the many who boast according to the flesh (2Cor 11:18), and those who would boast in the circumcised flesh of others (Gal 6:13).

In 2Cor 9:2 and 2Th 1:4 Paul boasts about a church to others: of the Corinthians' readiness to the Macedonians (2Cor 9:2), and of the Thessalonians' steadfastness and faith in persecution to the churches of God (2Th 1:4).

In 2Cor 10:8, 10:13, 10:15, 11:16, 11:18 (the second verb), 12:5 (the first verb) and 12:6 Paul's own boast is measured and qualified: of the authority the Lord gave (10:8), only within the area God assigned and not in others' labours (10:13, 10:15), a little and as a fool (11:16, 11:18), on behalf of the man caught up (12:5), and held back though it would be true (12:6).

In 2Cor 11:30, 12:5 (the second verb) and 12:9 the object of Paul's boast is his weakness: if he must boast it will be of what shows his weakness (11:30), on his own behalf only of weaknesses (12:5), and all the more gladly, because Christ's power is made perfect in weakness (12:9).
In Jam 1:9 the imperative tells the lowly brother to boast in his exaltation; with the rich told to do so in his humiliation (1:10), the ground of the boast is a reversal of standing.
In Jam 4:16 the present indicative (second plural) is a boast made in arrogance, about plans for tomorrow; the verse judges all such boasting evil.

In 2Cor 1:14 and 2Cor 5:12 the noun names a boast that people are to one another: on the day of the Lord the Corinthians are Paul's boast and he is theirs (2Cor 1:14), and Paul gives them cause to boast about him against those who boast of appearance (2Cor 5:12).
In Gal 6:4 the noun is a reason for boasting that comes from testing one's own work; it is then in oneself alone and not in comparison with a neighbour.
In 2Cor 1:12 the noun names what Paul boasts of: the testimony of his conscience that he behaved in simplicity and godly sincerity, by the grace of God and not by earthly wisdom.
In 1Cor 13:4 the verb (present, third singular) is denied of love: love does not vaunt itself; it stands between not envying and not being arrogant.

In 2Cor 11:21 the verb is 'to dare', twice: whatever anyone else dares, Paul too dares, speaking as a fool. The ESV adds 'to boast of' to both; the Greek says daring, and the boast is supplied from the context of 11:16-18.
In Psa 94:4 the verb of saying (imperfect, third plural) is rendered 'boast': all the evildoers speak of themselves, set in parallel with pouring out arrogant words.

In Psa 38:16 and Obd 12 the verb of making great is rendered 'boast': enemies make themselves great over the psalmist when his foot slips (Psa 38:16), and Edom is told not to do so over Judah in the day of distress (Obd 12). Both are a magnifying of oneself over one who falls.

In Psa 75:4 the code is the verb of being foolish or acting madly, rendered 'boastful' and 'Do not boast': God tells the boastful not to boast, in parallel with telling the wicked not to lift up the horn.

In 1Ki 20:11 and Pro 27:1 the jussive is negated: a boast made before the outcome is forbidden, of the man arming himself as though he had already taken his armour off (1Ki 20:11), and of tomorrow, which no one knows (Pro 27:1).

In Jer 9:23 the jussive is negated three times, each with its own ground: the wise man in his wisdom, the mighty in his might, the rich in his riches. Each ground is a real possession, and each is set aside as a ground for a boast.

In Psa 49:6 and Jer 49:4 the boast rests on wealth that is trusted: the abundance of riches (Psa 49:6), and the valleys and treasures of the faithless daughter, who says no one will come against her (Jer 49:4).
In Psa 52:1 the question to the mighty man asks why he boasts of evil, and the verse answers with God's steadfast love that endures all day.
In Psa 97:7 the participle names those who make their boast in worthless idols, the worshippers of images who are put to shame.

In Psa 34:2 and Jer 9:24 the boast is made in the Lord: the psalmist's soul boasts in him and the humble hear and are glad (Psa 34:2), and the one who boasts is to boast that he understands and knows the Lord (Jer 9:24).

In Isa 61:6 the code is the verb of exchanging (here: to enter into, to be changed into), rendered 'you shall boast' of the nations' glory. The Hebrew may say the people come into the nations' glory; the ESV reads it as a boast. Both readings are open; I read the ESV's as its rendering of entering into that glory.

In Judg 7:2 and Isa 10:15 the verb (to glorify oneself) is a claim over the one who did the work: Israel would glorify itself over the Lord, saying its own hand saved it (Judg 7:2), and the axe would glorify itself over the one who hews with it (Isa 10:15).

In Obd 12 the noun is 'mouth', joined with the verb of making great (boast|H1431 in this subgroup): Edom is told not to make its mouth great over Judah in the day of distress. The ESV renders the two words together as 'boast'.
In Isa 20:5 the noun of beauty or glory is rendered 'boast': Egypt was what Judah gloried in, set beside Cush its hope, and both end in dismay and shame.

For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24); The boast is in knowing God, and what is known is his character; The soul's boast. "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2, carried); Not in my bow. "For not in my bow do I trust ... In God we have boasted continually" (Psa 44:6–8). "Only in the Lord, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength ... In the Lord all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory" (Isa 45:24–25); The nations. If Israel returns and swears in truth, "nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory" (Jer 4:2); Exulting; "all who swear by him shall exult" (Psa 63:11); "Let the righteous one rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!" (Psa 64:10); "that I may glory with your inheritance" (Psa 106:5); The cross. "far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Gal 6:14); Christ, not the flesh. "glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh — though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also" (Php 3:3–4). Paul has standing in the flesh, "I have more", and sets it aside; Hope, sufferings, God. ESV renders kauchaomai "rejoice" here:; "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings" (Rom 5:2–3); "we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation" (5:11); The same word that elsewhere is a proud boast is here joy in hope, in suffering, and in God; Held fast. "if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope" (Heb 3:6); The conscience. "our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12). The boast is a clear conscience, and its ground is named as grace.

God is not the subject of a boast in these verses. He is its right object, and his character is what is boasted in. "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24). The proper boast is knowing God as he is: The boast is moved, not removed. The same impulse that boasts in wisdom, might and riches (Jer 9:23) is turned to God (9:24; 1Co 1:31). It becomes joy in hope and in suffering (Rom 5:2–3); I read: set beside batches 1–3, the human "lifting" is not abolished. Where it rests on oneself it is pride. Where it rests on God it is glory in him. This fits Ch 12 claim C-182 (the boast moved to what God does). It is a reconciliation point when that chapter is touched; Gift excludes self-boasting. "it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Eph 2:8–9). "What do you have that you did not receive?" (1Co 4:7). "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Gal 6:3); This is the researcher's "assumed" in the verses' words: a standing held as one's own when it was received, or thought when it is not so; The contrast with God, from batches 1–3, is that his standing is neither received nor assumed; The measure is assigned. "the area of influence God assigned to us" (2Co 10:13), and in batch 3 "the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3). I read: where God's height is his by nature, a person's rightful standing is a measure given, and pride boasts "beyond limits"; Christ's power in weakness. "my power is made perfect in weakness ... so that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2Co 12:9). The boast in weakness makes room for another's power. This bears on 13.1 Lowering himself, as in batch 3 §3.4; God's steadfast love answers the boast of evil. "Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day" (Psa 52:1). God's character is set over the mighty man's boast, as his mercy answered presumption in batch 2 §3.7.

The boast is moved, not removed: "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (Jer 9:24); "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31); The same word becomes joy in hope and in suffering (Rom 5:2–3, 11); Boasting in weakness: "so that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2Co 12:9); Boasting of others (2Co 7:4; 1Th 2:19); The boast within the measure God assigned (2Co 10:13), as thinking of oneself is within "the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3).

The Greek picture is swelling, physioō, "to inflate". In Paul it is set again and again against love: Knowledge. "This 'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1Co 8:1–3). Swelling knowledge is answered not by more knowledge but by being known by God; Love is not. "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant" (1Co 13:4). Before this: "if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge ... but have not love, I am nothing" (13:2); Party; "that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:6–7); Here Paul states what the Hebrew verses showed in story: pride holds what was received "as if you did not receive it"; Talk without power. "Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you ... I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power" (1Co 4:18–20). The arrogance rests on Paul being absent; Where grief belongs. "And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?" (1Co 5:2). Pride stands where mourning should be; Without reason. "puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head" (Col 2:18–19, carried from M09); The new convert. "He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6). The verse joins conceit to the devil's condemnation. It does not say what the devil's condemnation was. I read: it is held for 13.3 (other spirits). It is not built on here; Controversy. "he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension" (1Ti 6:4). Conceit is joined to understanding nothing, and to quarrels; With pleasure. "swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power" (2Ti 3:4–5); Among the others; "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Co 12:20); "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26), after "let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (5:25); Conceit is named among the things that set people against each other.

The given-or-taken line is stated outright. "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7): This is the plainest statement in the three batches of what the researcher suspected. Human pride holds as its own what was received; The researcher's word "assumed" fits: the standing is taken up as if it were not given; The right measure is the one God assigns. "not to think of himself more highly than he ought ... according to the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3). I read: where God has height by nature, a person has a measure by gift. Pride is thinking past the gift; Taking God's seat; "takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" (2Th 2:4); Together with Eze 28:2 and Isa 14:13 (batches 1–2), the verses show pride at its full height as a claim to God's own place; I read: God's "Most High" is the place pride reaches for. Batches 1–3 show no one holding it but God; Christ's firstness is grounded, and pleased; "that in everything he might be preeminent. For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell" (Col 1:18–19); His first place rests on what he is: before all things, the one through whom all were made, firstborn from the dead. It is not claimed against anyone; Batch 1 also has Christ's majesty as "received ... from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17), and his seat taken "after making purification for sins" (Heb 1:3); I read: in the verses the Son's height comes with his descent: firstborn from the dead, seated after purification. This bears on 13.1 Lowering himself; God's knowing is what pride meets. "God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God" (Luk 16:15). "he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts" (Luk 1:51). As in batch 2 (1Sa 2:3), God's knowledge is joined to his answer to pride; Other beings in these verses (held, not read in); A messenger of Satan is given against conceit (2Co 12:7); The conceited may fall "into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6); Angels greater in might do not blaspheme where the willful do (2Pe 2:11); These are for 13.2 and 13.3. findings.text: The one who boasts holds up a ground as his own and speaks of it: his wisdom, might and riches (Jer 9:23), trusted wealth (Psa 49:6), his own work set on the same terms as another's (2Cor 11:12), men (1Cor 3:21), a gift he never gives (Pro 25:14). The act is a claim of standing made from what one has or does.

God's word shuts the boast out: the Lord forbids it over wisdom, might and riches (Jer 9:23) and before the outcome (1Ki 20:11); no flesh may boast before him (1Cor 1:29); the boast is excluded by the law of faith, not by works (Rom 3:27, Eph 2:9); no one is to boast in men (1Cor 3:21); love does not boast (1Cor 13:4).

The ground of the boast can be a person or a state held before God rather than a possession: the church as Paul's crown at the Lord's coming (1Th 2:19, 2Cor 1:14), the testimony of conscience to conduct by grace (2Cor 1:12), the reason found in one's own tested work (Gal 6:4), the hope held fast with confidence (Heb 3:6), a ground Paul would rather die than lose, which preaching under necessity does not give (1Cor 9:15, 1Cor 9:16).

The boast is directed to the Lord as its ground: in God continually, with thanks (Psa 44:8), the soul's boast in the Lord that the humble hear and are glad at (Psa 34:2), understanding and knowing the Lord who practises steadfast love, justice and righteousness (Jer 9:24), in the Lord (1Cor 1:31, 2Cor 10:17), and only in the cross (Gal 6:14). God is the one boasted in, never the one who boasts.

parts.grounds: My soul makes its boast in the Lord

findings.text: The same act is refused or pursued by its ground: forbidden in wisdom, might and riches yet commanded in knowing the Lord (Jer 9:23 against Jer 9:24), excluded before God yet commanded in the Lord (1Cor 1:29 against 1Cor 1:31), and the lowly told to boast in a reversal (Jam 1:9). The boast is turned, not removed; the codes carry the turn as boast against rejoice or glory.

parts.grounds: let him who boasts boast in this

findings.text: The boast is made over another who is weaker, fallen or the giver: Moab and Ammon over God's people and land, with taunts (Zep 2:8, Zep 2:10), enemies over a man whose foot slips, with rejoicing (Psa 38:16), Edom over Judah in its day of distress (Obd 12), the boastful beside the wicked lifting the horn (Psa 75:4), and over God himself, crediting one's own hand (Judg 7:2), as the axe over the one who hews (Isa 10:15).

The boast can be made about others and held on their keeping: Paul boasts of a church's readiness and zeal to another (2Cor 9:2), of the Thessalonians' steadfastness and faith in affliction to the churches (2Th 1:4), sends brothers so it is not empty (2Cor 9:3), asks for proof of their love and his boast (2Cor 8:24), and holds a mutual boast for the day of the Lord (2Cor 1:14). Its truth rests on their conduct (2Cor 7:14).

The boast comes out as speech and words: arrogant words poured out (Psa 94:4), the mouth speaking swollen things (Jude 16), the tongue boasting of great things (Jam 3:5), sayings approved after the foolish (Psa 49:13), boasts the Lord declares false (Jer 48:30), and the boast of a gift never given (Pro 25:14).

parts.grounds: They pour out their arrogant words

findings.text: Truth and shame qualify whether the boast holds: boasts false and false to the truth (Jer 48:30, Jam 3:14), boasting not good (1Cor 5:6), a boast that proved true and was not put to shame (2Cor 7:14), boasting bound to the truth of Christ (2Cor 11:10), the law boasted in while broken, dishonouring God (Rom 2:23), and shame on those whose boast was idols or Egypt (Psa 97:7, Isa 20:5).

Measure qualifies Paul's own boast: a little (2Cor 11:16), not beyond the area God assigned nor in others' labours (2Cor 10:13, 2Cor 10:15), of authority given for building up, not destroying (2Cor 10:8), and held back so that no one thinks more of him than is seen (2Cor 12:6). The limit is set by what was assigned and what others see.

parts.grounds: we will not boast beyond limits

findings.text: Paul's boast is made under necessity and of weakness: he must boast (2Cor 11:30, 2Cor 12:1), with nothing gained by it (2Cor 12:1), dares as a fool though too weak (2Cor 11:21), and boasts all the more gladly of his weaknesses after the word that grace suffices and power is made perfect in weakness (2Cor 12:9).

What God gives comes first and the boast follows from it: grace (2Cor 1:12), authority the Lord gave (2Cor 10:8), the area God assigned (2Cor 10:13), the exaltation of the lowly (Jam 1:9), the people called priests who come into the nations' glory (Isa 61:6). The boast as though one had not received is questioned (1Cor 4:7).

parts.grounds: which the Lord gave for building you up

findings.text: The heart's condition qualifies the boast: where bitter jealousy and selfish ambition are in the heart the boast is forbidden and joined to being false to the truth (Jam 3:14), set against the meekness of wisdom in the verse before.

findings.text: Those who boast are named the wicked, the evildoers and the faithless, and the boast stands beside the desires of the soul, greed that renounces the Lord, and favouritism for gain: the wicked boasts of his soul's desires (Psa 10:3), the evildoers boast (Psa 94:4), the mighty man boasts of evil (Psa 52:1), the faithless daughter boasts (Jer 49:4), boasters follow their desires (Jude 16).

The boast can rest on the flesh and the outward appearance rather than the heart: those who boast of appearance and not of the heart (2Cor 5:12), the many who boast according to the flesh (2Cor 11:18), and those who would boast in others' circumcised flesh while not keeping the law themselves (Gal 6:13).
Trust and boast are linked on the same ground: trust in wealth and boast in riches (Psa 49:6), boast of valleys and trust in treasures with no one to come against her (Jer 49:4).
